questions.stem: State the reaction studied and its catalyst.
questions.modelAnswer: The iodination of propanone, catalysed by dilute sulfuric acid.

questions.stem: State the quenching agent and the titration used for the removed samples.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium hydrogencarbonate quenches, and titration against thiosulfate(VI) with starch reads the iodine.

questions.stem: Explain why quenching is essential before titrating a removed sample.
questions.modelAnswer: An unquenched sample keeps reacting during handling and titration, so the iodine measured would belong to the analysis moment rather than the removal moment, corrupting the time-concentration pair.

questions.stem: A student quenches each sample but forgets the starch indicator until near the endpoint. What difficulty follows?
questions.modelAnswer: Iodine's own colour is faint at low concentration, so without starch the endpoint creeps up blurred; adding starch late still colours the residual iodine sharply, but the student risks overshooting and should redo the titration for accuracy.

questions.stem: State the order of the reaction with respect to iodine.
questions.modelAnswer: Zero order, proved by the straight-line concentration-time graph.

questions.stem: State the full rate equation for the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone.
Explain how a constant gradient on the concentration-time graph proves zero order.
questions.modelAnswer: The gradient of a concentration-time curve is the instantaneous rate; a constant gradient therefore means a rate that does not change while iodine's concentration falls, which is only possible if the rate does not depend on iodine concentration - the definition of zero order.

questions.stem: Predict what happens to the measured rate if the acid concentration is doubled while propanone and iodine stay fixed.
questions.modelAnswer: The rate equation carries [H+] to the first power, so doubling the acid doubles the rate, even though the iodine curve itself stays straight.
